articles.title: Michael and Susan Dell's foundation backs free skills training in Texas; a 2026 update reports that 78% of Skillpoint Alliance graduates find jobs and average monthly earnings reach $3,600
articles.summary: The philanthropic organisation founded by Michael Dell and Susan Dell has spotlighted the growing impact of free skilled-trades training in Texas,
articles.body: The philanthropic organisation founded by Michael Dell and Susan Dell has spotlighted the growing impact of free skilled-trades training in Texas, reporting that a large majority of participants secure employment shortly after completing the programme. According to a 2026 update from the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, 78% of graduates from Skillpoint Alliance find jobs after completing their training, while graduates earn an average of $3,600 per month and increase their earnings by an average of 150%.How the training worksSkillpoint’s pitch is speed and a direct link to employers. Traditional training programmes, the foundation notes, often take months or years, cost thousands of dollars and may not lead to available jobs. Skillpoint instead builds its free five-week courses with employers who are hiring now, so participants train for open positions companies need to fill today.Participants earn industry-recognised certifications, visit job sites and train on electrical systems, HVAC equipment and plumbing installations designed to mirror real working conditions. They also receive mentoring and help with job placement.Industry certifications and job placement supportParticipants in the programme receive hands-on training, earn industry-recognised certifications, visit job sites and receive mentoring and job placement assistance. According to the organisation, employer partnerships shape every aspect of the curriculum, creating a more direct pathway from training to employment. The results have been significant. The foundation reports that more than three-quarters of graduates secure jobs after completing the programme, while many move into careers that offer greater stability, higher wages and long-term advancement opportunities.Addressing Texas' skilled worker shortageThe programme comes as Texas continues to face growing demand for skilled workers across critical industries. According to the foundation, many employers struggle to fill essential roles, while adults seeking career advancement often face barriers such as lengthy training periods and high educational costs.The organisation highlighted the story of a graduate named Mariah, who transitioned from security work into an HVAC technician role after completing five weeks of training. She now works as a start-up technician, inspecting and testing newly installed HVAC systems before they reach customers.Expansion planned across Central TexasTo meet growing demand, Skillpoint Alliance is expanding its operations in South Austin and New Braunfels. The organisation is further planning to increase the training capacity by updating the families, hiring more instructors and support staff and also running multiple cohorts. The Michael & Susan Dell Foundation claimed that the expansion is aimed at helping more Texans gain access to fast, employer-connected training programmes that can lead to stable careers and improved economic mobility while helping businesses fill critical workforce gaps.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink, Starshield connections return to normal speeds after weeklong disruption
articles.summary: Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems are operating at speeds exceeding 400 km/h, the country's defence minister said on
articles.body: Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems are operating at speeds exceeding 400 km/h, the country's defence minister said on Saturday, after more than a week of service disruptions that hit military operations.“The ministry of defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable,” defence minister Evhenii Khmara told reporters.Ukraine relies on SpaceX's civilian Starlink satellite network and its military-grade Starshield system to support military communications and operations, including efforts to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.The Ukrainian defence ministry said its monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the services, but that speed metrics had now returned to normal. However, it did not confirm whether service had been fully restored, Reuters reported.Khmara also highlighted the importance of the recovery for military operations.“This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications,” he said, according to AFP.The restrictions, first reported on October 14, affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted communications along the front line, Ukrainian officials said, according to Reuters. Sources told the news agency that connection speeds had fallen to around 160 km/h or lower.The satellite network has become a point of tension between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had previously accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn Kyiv about incoming missile strikes and weakening Ukraine's military response by throttling Starlink speeds, AFP reported.Khmara credited Zelenskyy's “firm stance” on the issue, saying it was “bearing fruit”, AFP reported.The disruption followed US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to buy Russian diesel and his decision to waive new sanctions on Moscow, while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, Reuters reported.On Friday, Trump said that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out”.You use AI every day. articles.title: In a first, forest staff from 6 states to get Israeli Krav Maga training to tackle forest crimes
articles.summary: Uttarakhand Forestry Training Academy to train 170 forest staff from 6 states and J&K in Israeli Krav Maga from Nov to tackle forest crimes and attacks.
articles.body: Dehradun: In a first for India’s frontline forest personnel, Uttarakhand Forestry Training Academy (UFTA) in Haldwani will introduce Krav Maga, an Israeli self-defence technique, into its training curriculum from Nov to help staff tackle attacks by timber and sand mafias, poachers and forest encroachers. Around 170 foresters and forest rangers from six states and Jammu & Kashmir will undergo training in the unarmed combat system, which focuses on responding to real-life threats, including assaults involving weapons and multiple attackers. The academy introduced the initiative after an internal assessment found that around 60 frontline forest personnel had lost their lives in the line of duty in Uttarakhand.UFTA director Sanjiv Chaturvedi said the two-month programme would cover around 130 foresters from Uttarakhand and Punjab, currently undergoing training at the academy, and 40 forest rangers from Jammu & Kashmir, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Madhya Pradesh. “The training will commence for two months starting November,” he said. Certified Krav Maga instructors, who have previously trained police and customs personnel at National Police Academy in Hyderabad and in Mumbai, will conduct the sessions. Officials said only five to six certified instructors of the technique were currently available in India.The academy, which has trained frontline forest personnel since 1979, decided to introduce Krav Maga after examining fatalities involving staff confronting timber and sand mafias, encroachers and other offenders. Its assessment documented particularly violent incidents, including one in which a forest official was burnt alive and another in which an official’s body parts were severed. Officials said such attacks highlighted the need to equip field personnel with practical defensive skills alongside conventional enforcement training. The technique had previously been taught to police and customs personnel and probationary IAS officers.The first phase, beginning in Nov, will involve two weeks of intensive practice in defending against single and multiple attackers, including those carrying sticks, axes, knives, sharp-edged weapons and firearms. The second phase, scheduled for Dec, will focus on defensive manoeuvres in dense forests, on uneven ground and in poor visibility. Trainees will also practise techniques to escape when surrounded and to disarm assailants while minimising the risk of injury.Academy officials said the programme aimed to reduce casualties during enforcement operations and improve personnel’s ability to respond swiftly to threats from organised forest crime. UFTA will meet the initial expenditure from funds allocated for training at state forest training academies.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Aries, Weekly Horoscope, October 25 to October 31, 2026: Charm brings success, but patience keeps you grounded
articles.summary: General: The week opens on a bright note, Aries, and you’ll feel it almost at once. Early in the week, your presence carries weight.
articles.body: General:The week opens on a bright note, Aries, and you’ll feel it almost at once. Early in the week, your presence carries weight. People listen when you speak, and even casual conversations can turn in your favour. There is a social warmth around you, like a clear morning after sticky weather. Family cheer also lifts your mood, and some of you may attend a gathering, small celebration, or community event that reminds you how much goodwill you’ve built over time. You’ll notice that your words have extra charm now. Use that gift gently, because one kind sentence can smooth an old wrinkle.Still, this isn’t a week for acting only on impulse. Beneath the applause and easy wins, there is a thread of confusion. You may second guess yourself even after making the right call. Strange, isn’t it? Outward respect, inward wobble. By the middle of the week, courage rises and you may feel tempted to take on an unusual task, make a sudden trip, or chase an idea simply because it excites you. Do it with open eyes. Delay any big purchase linked with travel or machinery. The second half asks for patience, hard work, and a steady hand. Restlessness may creep in, especially if your schedule fills up with errands, family obligations, or unfinished tasks.As the weekend approaches, your world becomes more local and personal. Neighbours, siblings, old friends, and familiar faces matter more than grand plans. A new friendship may begin in a simple setting, perhaps over tea, a family visit, or a nearby celebration. At the same time, don’t scatter your energy. Keep your feet on the ground, your meals simple, and your driving careful. This week rewards the Aries who can balance fire with common sense.Love and Relationships:Your emotional weather changes more than once this week. In the first part, family ties feel warmer and more cooperative. A spouse or partner may step in helpfully with domestic matters, and relatives seem more willing to support your plans. If you are single, you’re likely to attract people through conversation rather than drama. Your voice carries softness early in the week, and that can win hearts faster than any grand display. A family event or social visit may also bring a pleasant introduction. Nothing too filmi, but enough to make you smile on the way home.Midweek needs care. There is a clear sign of friction with a spouse or partner, mostly because both sides want to be heard first. Hot words come quickly for you now. Once spoken, they hang in the room like smoke. If a small disagreement starts over routine matters, travel, spending, timing, or who forgot what, don’t keep feeding it. Step back. Drink water. Come back later. The good news is that this tension doesn’t define the whole week. It passes if you refuse to turn every irritation into a battle.Toward the weekend, relationships settle into a more ordinary rhythm. Not dramatic, not cold, simply manageable. That’s not a bad thing. Married natives may find comfort in practical teamwork, especially around the house or while dealing with relatives. Children bring encouraging news or make you proud through effort and results. An old friend may reappear, and with that meeting comes a reminder of who has stood by you through different seasons. Hold on to those bonds. They are quieter than passion, but often much stronger.Education and Career:This week begins with promise in both career and studies. If you run a business, orders, enquiries, or client interest can increase early on, and not always from expected places. Doors open through reputation, referrals, and word of mouth. People trust your capability. That matters. Those in service or office roles may also find that seniors notice their reliability. If there’s a presentation, meeting, public dealing, or negotiation in the first half, go in prepared. You’re likely to leave a better impression than you realise.Students also have a supportive current this week. The mind is especially receptive in the early and later parts of the week, so this is a good time to revise, clear pending work, and ask teachers the questions you’ve been postponing. Midweek, your courage grows, but concentration may become patchy. You’ll want to attempt something difficult, perhaps a competitive topic, a new project, or a demanding subject. Good. Just don’t skip the basics. A bold mind still needs a timetable. Keep your study desk clean and your phone away for fixed hours. Simple discipline will help more than bursts of motivation.By Thursday onward, hard work becomes the real story. Results don’t come free. You may feel tense, lazy one moment and determined the next. That back and forth can be tiring. Yet a brave decision taken now can shape the next few weeks well, especially if it concerns workload, deadlines, or a practical change in routine. Support from a younger sibling or someone junior may unexpectedly strengthen your confidence. Keep going, even if progress looks slow. This week respects effort more than speed.Money and Finance:Money matters begin on a hopeful note. You may receive income from different sources, and there is a sense of financial satisfaction early in the week. If you are in business, fresh orders can improve your cash flow. If you are employed, side earnings, delayed payments, or family support may lighten your mind. There is also a favourable breeze for speculation, but only if you think before moving. Don’t bet on excitement. Don’t follow noise. You may hear many opinions around you, and strangely, this is one week when your own confidence may wobble even while luck is supporting you.Midweek and later, the tone changes. Financial progress continues, but it becomes clearly linked to hard work. Money won’t fall into your lap. It will come because you chased a payment, finished a task, accepted extra work, or stayed disciplined when others became lazy. That’s the real lesson here. Also, postpone a vehicle purchase for now. The timing is not clean, and there may be hidden stress around maintenance, paperwork, or sudden expense. Better to wait than regret.The weekend brings social spending temptations, especially if there is a neighbourly function or informal get together. Keep your wallet closed if the spending is only for show. You do not need to prove your generosity every time someone calls. Food outside should also be limited, partly for health and partly because small casual expenses can pile up this week. Save where you can. Spend where it counts. That simple line will protect you.Health and Well-being:Your energy is uneven this week, Aries. Early on, the spirit feels bright, but the body sends smaller warnings. The right eye may trouble some of you, especially from screen strain, lack of sleep, or too much time in bright light. Don’t ignore it. Midweek is more delicate. You may feel daring and physically capable, yet this is exactly when overexertion, rushing, or careless travel can tire you out. Short journeys need planning. If you are driving, stay alert. If you are riding with someone else, avoid last minute chaos and leave on time.Stress builds quietly from Thursday onward. Hard work, mental agitation, and unfinished responsibilities can make you restless. Then comes laziness, not because you are weak, but because the body wants recovery. Listen to that signal. Sleep on time. Eat warm, simple food. Skip outside snacks for a few days, especially over the weekend, because digestion looks sensitive. If you’ve been promising yourself a healthier routine, this is the week to start with very small things. A morning walk. Less caffeine. More water. Nothing fancy.Emotionally too, you’ll need cooling methods. Arguments with a spouse or pressure from work can sit in your chest longer than you admit. Don’t carry every irritation like a badge. Speak less when angry. Breathe before replying. Meet an old friend if the chance comes, because familiar company can ground you beautifully now. By the weekend, the best medicine is simplicity, home food, careful travel, and enough rest to calm your racing mind.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. articles.title: Omar Abdullah to MLAs: Stop sending WhatsApp messages, knocking on my and Farooq’s doors for ministerial berths; opposition calls it ‘cult of self’
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah, after meeting Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Saturday, said a cabinet expansion was on the
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah, after meeting Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Saturday, said a cabinet expansion was on the cards and urged party colleagues to stop sending him lengthy WhatsApp messages and book-length profiles seeking ministerial berths.He also advised them against knocking on his door or that of his father and National Conference president, Dr Farooq Abdullah, to lobby for ministerial positions. The opposition described Omar’s portrayal of his party MLAs as demeaning to the political class and called it “the cult of self”.“The lieutenant governor sahab returned to Srinagar. In the meantime, his health had not been good, so I wanted to inquire about his well-being. There are also several issues on which it was necessary to meet him and seek his opinion from time to time. It had been a long time since I met him, so I sought an appointment today. He gave me time,” Omar told reporters after meeting the LG.“I know you people are not interested in anything else. You want to know whether I discussed the cabinet reshuffle with the LG sahab. Yes, absolutely. I sought an appointment with him for the expansion (of cabinet) and requested him to fix a time in the first two or three days of next week. So that I will make some changes and expand my council of ministers,” Omar said.He said the LG would fix a time for the process.“Now that I have told you about the reshuffle, I want to make a request to my colleagues, as news might have already spread about next week’s reshuffle. There is no need to knock on Farooq Abdullah’s door, my door or anyone else’s door,” Omar said.“The decision about who will become a minister has been taken. I request my colleagues to be patient. What is destined for them will happen. First, it is in God’s hands and then we took the decision. Whoever is destined to become a minister will become one. But please, do not knock on doors now. Do not send me WhatsApp messages,” he said.“I am receiving so many WhatsApp messages, with people writing lengthy resumes and sending me entire books. It is as if I do not know these people. They are sending me their complete biodata, as though I am not already familiar with them,” he said.“So please, do not send WhatsApp messages, call or knock on doors. Whatever has to happen will happen in the next two or three days,” Omar said.Omar was sworn in on Oct 16, 2024, along with five ministers, including deputy CM Surinder Choudhary. At present, three cabinet berths remain vacant. Under the norms, the strength of the council of ministers cannot exceed 10% of the total strength of the assembly. The J&K assembly has 90 members, capping the council of ministers at nine.Omar has allocated deputy CM Surinder Kumar Choudhary the portfolios of public works, industries and commerce, mining, labour and skill development. Sakeena Itoo handles health and medical education, school education, higher education and social welfare. Javed Ahmed Rana oversees water resources, forests, environment and tribal affairs. Javid Ahmad Dar is tasked with agriculture, panchayati raj and cooperatives. Satish Sharma is responsible for food, consumer affairs, transport, science and IT, youth affairs, sports and training.Leader of Opposition and BJP's Sunil Sharma, who has been claiming that the NC will "implode" if Omar goes ahead with the cabinet expansion, said, “The CM is behaving like a king. Like a king, he doesn’t like people visiting his home. He wants only a close coterie around him, with everyone else reduced to reporting to them. He is out to demean his own MLAs and has repeatedly humiliated them inside and outside the Assembly,” he added.Peoples Conference chairman Sajad Lone sharply reacted to Omar’s statement, calling it “the cult of self”.“I watched CM sahib talking to the media after meeting LG sahib. What a contemptuous and disdainful way of asking his party MLAs to not pester him for a ministerial berth. I honestly can’t believe that these MLAs are comfortable with such belittling and humiliating remarks,” Lone said.“If you are unable to accommodate them in the cabinet, you can spare them from public humiliation,” he added.“Anyway, these are internal party matters and I should not have commented. But there is always a spillover. You may direct the derision at your own members, but it invariably belittles the political class. I wonder how these elected members face their electors when they know they are treated like unworthy and incapable schoolboys,” Lone added.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: I could have rescued my daughter from disappointment. Here's why I didn't
articles.summary: A child psychologist explains why rescuing kids from disappointment undermines self-efficacy, coping skills, and long-term child resilience.
articles.body: A few weeks ago, my daughter came home from second grade, and she told me she wasn’t invited to her friend Samantha’s birthday party. I asked her if she knew how many kids were invited, and she told me twenty. I was incensed. It was a big party, not a small, exclusive gathering, and my baby was left out. I knew that, in that moment, I could do two things: acknowledge that being left out hurts, or pick up the phone and call Samantha’s mom to secure an invitation. I had to deliberately focus on the former and stop myself from instinctually choosing the latter because, these days, it seems like we are all defaulting to the phone call. The instinct is understandable. We all hate watching our children suffer. But we need to remember that there is a clear difference between supporting our children through disappointment and making sure they never experience it. OUR KIDS AREN’T BROKEN. WE NEED TO STOP TREATING EVERY STRUGGLE LIKE A DISORDER It seems like we have lost our ability to tolerate ordinary childhood struggles. We pathologize and diagnose every negative experience—sadness becomes depression, meanness becomes bullying, and frustration becomes emotional dysregulation. And each unsavory, undesirable part of life becomes an intervention target. Parents feel pressure to act rather than simply let life unfold. But the reality is that life is messy and often uncomfortable, and not every negative emotion is evidence of a problem that requires us to intervene. Emotional discomfort isn’t inherently dangerous, and, in fact, negative experiences can serve important developmental functions. Coping with adversity helps kids recognize what matters to them, adjust expectations, solve problems, and navigate relationships. When we have a myopic focus on protecting children’s mental health, we often forget that mental health is based not on the absence of negative emotions but on our ability to handle them. As parents, we must remember that resilience requires practice, and competence develops through experience. Children build coping skills when they encounter manageable challenges, experiment with solutions, and discover that they can tolerate discomfort. And all this requires the possibility of failure. Children never develop the ability to recover from disappointment if they don’t have the opportunity to feel it. I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE Parents have a key role to play in the development of self-efficacy. We communicate our expectations about what they can do. When we give our children space to learn and grow, we communicate that they can handle challenges on their own. On the flip side, when we repeatedly intervene to solve their problems, we send the message that they can’t do it without us. It’s impossible to teach kids to swim by keeping them out of the water! Children never develop the ability to recover from disappointment if they don’t have the opportunity to feel it. Constantly rescuing our kids has three unintended consequences. First, it undermines self-efficacy. Children look to adults to solve problems rather than trusting themselves and discovering their own resourcefulness. Second, it reinforces avoidance. Children learn that unpleasant emotions are intolerable rather than temporary experiences that they can manage. Third, it creates unrealistic expectations. Children learn to expect the world to accommodate their preferences rather than learning to manage unfairness, frustration, rejection, and disappointment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Of course, children often need support. Removing demands may, at times, be necessary. But when we reflexively remove demands instead of helping children develop the capacity to navigate them, we prioritize short-term relief over long-term growth. We must deliberately support our children without constantly rescuing them. First, we should validate the feeling without catastrophizing it. Acknowledge the disappointment, but don’t amplify it into a crisis. Second, resist the urge to solve the problem. Before intervening, ask whether it is something your child can reasonably navigate independently. Third, help your child develop their own solutions. You can ask them what they could do next or what they might try differently next time, but remember that sometimes the best intervention is no intervention at all. Sometimes children just need time to feel bad and move on. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When I think about my own daughter and that birthday party, I wonder if maybe this will give her the opportunity and motivation to make a new friend. Maybe she’ll learn to cope with exclusion. Maybe she’ll just feel bummed for the afternoon and move on. All are developmentally meaningful (and desirable) outcomes. And I remember that my job isn’t to eliminate adversity and disappointment; it’s to help her become a person who can handle the struggles that are inevitably part of life. I don’t want to raise someone who never falls down; I want to raise someone who knows how to get back up. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR. KATIE DAVIS

articles.title: German police detain suspect after fire engulfs Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest
articles.summary: No injuries were reported at the building, while police said a ‘suspicious person’ had been taken into custody.
articles.body:
German police have detained a suspect after a fire engulfed the Eagle’s Nest, Adolf Hitler’s notorious Nazi-era mountain retreat in Bavaria, prompting an overnight emergency operation involving about 200 firefighters.

No injuries were reported at the building, known locally as the Kehlsteinhaus. Police said investigators were examining whether a “suspicious person” taken into temporary custody was connected to the blaze.

The fire alarm was triggered by a smoke detector at about 9:50pm (19:50 GMT) on Friday. Emergency crews could see flames rising above the building as they approached and found it “completely ablaze”, according to police.

The retreat’s remote Alpine location, at an altitude of more than 1,800 metres (about 6,000 feet), complicated efforts to extinguish the fire, police spokesperson Lisa Maier said.

While authorities have not announced a cause, German media reported that investigators suspected arson.

The newspaper Bild said emergency responders had encountered a motorcyclist travelling towards them on their way to the scene and that he was subsequently detained. His possible involvement remained under investigation.

Maier said inquiries were continuing, with police planning a news conference later on Saturday.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the stone-and-granite retreat stands on the Kehlstein mountain above Obersalzberg, near Berchtesgaden in southern Germany.

Designed as a monument to Hitler’s rule and a setting for receiving foreign diplomats, it offers sweeping views across the Bavarian Alps. Hitler himself visited the resort.

The site, which remains part of the legacy of Nazi Germany, survived World War II undamaged. It has operated as a restaurant since 1952 and also houses an exhibition examining its Nazi history.

articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink is back to normal after limits hobbled its drones
articles.summary: KYIV — Ukraine said on Saturday ​that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were again operating at high speeds after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with ⁠the US.
articles.body: KYIV — Ukraine said on Saturday ​that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were again operating at high speeds after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with ⁠the US. Problems with Elon Musk’s SpaceX-owned systems came after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions hampered ⁠the military’s ability to intercept Russian ​attack ⁠drones and forced the cancellation of some operations. “Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence monitoring systems are officially recording the restoration of ⁠Starlink/Starshield operating speeds,” the ministry said on the Telegram app. “Connectivity remains ​stable ⁠at speeds exceeding 400 km ‌per hour,” it added. The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems’ maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether ‌service had been fully restored. When ‌limitations were in place, Ukraine experienced problems trying to operate at speeds over 160 kph. Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian ⁠territory, but Starlink is vital for frontline communications and Starshield is used for military operations in occupied territories. Limitations order The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence. Neither Musk nor the U.S. government has acknowledged responsibility ‌for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said ​publicly that any such decision could only have been ‌taken by the other. Reuters has ⁠reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from ⁠inside the White House. Previously, U.S. administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn ‌Starlink on or ​off in various countries, sources said. Trump ‌said on Friday that if ​problems persisted, he would “get it straightened out.”

articles.title: More than 100 detained in France as thousands protest in Paris
articles.summary: European countries have been bracing for discontent this weekend, with thousands of people taking to the streets. Follow for the latest updates.
articles.body:
• Fresh protests: France’s Interior Ministry says at least 135 people have been detained in connection with today’s protests now sweeping the country. A march attended by thousands in Paris has so far passed by largely peacefully , but tear gas has been deployed in three cities .

• Security operation: Some 70,000 officers have been positioned across the country this weekend as part of a huge security operation . The city of Nice has deployed the largest number of police officers in its history to attend today’s demonstrations.

• Discontent in the continent: Anti-government demonstrations are also taking place in a number of other European countries. Police in Albania have been pictured deploying water cannon during clashes with protesters, while stores have been boarded up in Italy ahead of an expected march.

After a peaceful march through Paris, a crowd of several thousand protestors confronted police, who used tear gas and a water cannon to block them, according to a CNN team at the scene.

The clashes broke out at the Porte de Vincennes, the end-point of the march, which drew an estimated 110,000 people.

The protesters, mostly young and dressed in black congregated in front of police lines leading to Place de la Nation, where the organizers had originally intended to end the march.

With a police helicopter hovering overhead, police started using tear gas and a water cannon in an effort to move the protesters back. There was a defiant mood in the crowd, with a handful of protesters targeting the police with lasers. Groups of young people were seen dancing with music pounding through the crowd as meters away tear gas billowed into the air.

Images from Bordeaux on France’s Atlantic coast show tear gas being used against protesters in the famous Place de la Bourse in the city’s historic center.

Videos show some masked protesters hurling objects at police as the tear gas drifts across the square.

Regional authorities said in a post on X that “hostile groups are attacking law enforcement, throwing projectiles, and setting up barricades at Place de la Bourse.” The post warns the public to avoid the area.

Live coverage by CNN affiliate BFMTV showed a tense stand-off between riot police and several hundred protesters on the bank of the River Gironde.

Today’s protests in the French capital of Paris have largely been peaceful so far, in contrast to those seen last Saturday, a senior police officer told CNN affiliate BFMTV.

“For the moment, the situation is pretty much under control, apart from some attempts to block the peripherique, which we stopped,” said Olivier Bourde, the Paris police force’s deputy director for public order, as he stood with his colleagues dressed in riot gear.

Hundreds of protesters have been shouting “ACAB,” a commonly used acronym for an anti-police slogan, a CNN producer in Paris heard.

Bourde couldn’t yet estimate when the protest would be over.

“Last week, we finished at 2 a.m. Now, it will depend on the if the protesters disperse normally, like a normal protest, or if we have breakaway groups,” he said.

CNN’s Joseph Ataman contributed reporting.

The leader of the far-left party France Insoumise has described the march through Paris as a “total victory for the social movement.”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the march, said on X : “The march gathered at the newly authorized location and is now moving forward peacefully, stretching over more than four kilometers.”

Live video showed many thousands walking through the streets, despite a last-minute order by authorities changing the route of the march.

“The attempts by the Prefect of Police and (Prime Minister Sebastien) Lecornu to incite disorder have failed completely,” Mélenchon said.

“It is time for the authorities to yield; otherwise, the only option left to them will soon be the exit door,” he added. praising the discipline of the marchers.

Melenchon has championed the demands of high school students and earlier Saturday warned President Emmanuel Macron that it was time for him to give in to their demands for more investment in France’s schools.

“After that, all he’ll have left is the exit door,” he said.

As scores of protesters take to the streets in cities across France today, anti-government demonstrations are also taking place in a number of other European countries.

Protesters in Tirana, Albania , set fire to dumpsters and threw stones and tear gas canisters, according to photographs taken by Reuters.

Chair cushions which had been symbolically offered to protesters as an invitation for a dialogue were also set alight in front of a government building, according to the outlet.

One man was photographed lying on the ground in front of a police vehicle, while other protesters waved Albanian flags outside of the country’s Ministry of Education.

Police deployed water cannons to spray demonstrators near the ministry building, photos showed.

In Brussels, Belgium , student held up placards and barricaded streets. Police deployed a water cannon, according to public broadcaster VRT.

A police officer was photographed by Reuters spraying a substance at demonstrators. VRT reported that the police had deployed both pepper spray and tear gas.

In the Italian cities of Naples, Rome and Milan, stores boarded up their windows ahead of planned protests.

A CNN reporter on the ground in Rome said that a march began peacefully around 3 p.m. local time (9 a.m. ET). Many protesters waved Italian flags as they walked.

Police have used tear gas in the northern city of Lille in a confrontation with hundreds of protesters.

Videos showed police charging dozens of protesters, many of whom were wearing face masks. The demonstrators fell back and then regrouped.

Within the last few minutes, clashes began in the southern port city of Marseille, according to live coverage on CNN affiliate BFMTV. Riot police used tear gas there too.

Tensions were also running high in the southeastern city of Nice on the Mediterranean coast, where police tried to disperse demonstrators in the center of the city, using loudspeakers to order people to evacuate the area.

Tear gas was also deployed for more than an hour earlier in Lyon in central France, as scattered groups moved from street to street.

The regional authorities said that “several groups of individuals with hostile intentions were preparing to commit acts of violence and vandalism by masking and hooding themselves.”

“After warnings and demands for dispersal, with no reaction from the demonstrators, law enforcement used tear gas measures,” the Prefect of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region said on X.

“Internal security forces were targeted by numerous projectile throws, including iron pellets. These individuals began erecting barricades,” it added.

Nationwide industrial action will take place in France on November 5 if French President Emmanuel Macron does not respond to the demands of protesters, the leader of far-left party La France Insoumise has warned.

“A general strike, called by the CGT, looms over the government for the 5th of November,” Jean-Luc Mélenchon told CNN’s French affiliate BFMTV from the frontline of today’s demonstration in Paris, adding: “The masses will be set in motion.”

Mélenchon said Macron risks the industrial action that he said would create “far more hazardous conditions” for the president unless he “gives in now.”

Some context: Some protesters have been calling for greater investment in the country’s education system, more opportunities for its youth workforce and solutions to its surging living costs.

Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise party has backed the student movement which has been a part of the protests sweeping France.

With protests underway in several cities across France, there have been clashes between police and protestors in the city of Lyon.

Live coverage from CNN affiliate BFMTV showed police using tear gas in central Lyon in an effort to disperse protestors wearing masks, some of whom picked up tear gas grenades and threw them back at police lines.

The clashes occurred around the Place Jean Macé, near Lyon university.

Elsewhere in the city, there was a stand-off between riot police and hundreds of demonstrators, according to live pictures.

“Some individuals, wearing hoods and masks, attempted to enter the restricted zone,” and “formal warnings were issued,” a source from the prefecture told BFMTV.

These individuals have since “split into two groups” and are currently being tracked by law enforcement, the source said. Police are intervening “whenever there is an attempt to set up barricades or when projectiles are thrown.”

Several peaceful protests are underway across France, with TV footage showing thousands of demonstrators marching in the cities of Marseille, Lyon and Lille.

Elsewhere, protests are also underway in Paris and took place in Orléans.

At least 135 people have been detained so far across France in connection with today’s protests, the country’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has said.

Speaking to CNN affiliate BFMTV, Nuñez said the detentions had all taken place before 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).

Nuñez also discussed the authorities’ decision to change planned protest routes in Paris and Orléans today, saying the changes were decided upon last night for good reason.

A protest march is now underway in Paris , with 70,000 police officers expected to be deployed across the country this weekend.

Specialist SWAT units, helicopters, armored vehicles, police dogs and water cannons are at the ready to be deployed as part of the operation, after more than half a million took to the streets last Saturday.

Police in Paris have already conducted hundreds of control checks in the Île-de-France region, seizing items including a knife, an angle grinder and protective gear such as face masks and diving goggles in the run up to the demonstrations.

Yesterday evening, the Paris police banned the original protest route for today, which would have taken the protest from the Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation. Unions appealed this decision in court, but the appeal was rejected.

A police spokesperson told CNN affiliate BFMTV the changes to the route were made in response to “evolving threats,” and influenced by what French President Emmanuel Macron described as a “ terrorist” attack in a Paris suburb yesterday in which one person was shot dead.

Separately, thousands of protesters have gathered in the French city of Orléans today to protest against the far-right National Rally party , which is holding its congress there this weekend.

CNN’s Joseph Ataman, Ivana Kottasová, Elina Baudier Kim, Charlotte Reck, Issy Ronald and Pierre Bairin contributed to this reporting.

The French city of Nice has deployed the largest number of police officers in its history to attend today’s demonstrations, the city mayor told CNN’s French affiliate BFMTV earlier.

“We have mobilized close to 310 municipal police officers, which is unprecedented in the history of the municipal police of Nice,” Éric Ciotti said earlier.

In total, there will be more than 700 security personnel on the streets of the waterfront city throughout the day, Ciotti said, tasked with protecting citizens and businesses.

While France is no stranger to mass protests and strikes, the latest wave of demonstrations is different, Michael Froman, the president of the Council on Foreign Relations, said.

Writing for US-based think tank’s website , Froman said the protests stem from a “fundamental collapse of the French social contract.”

Froman added the protests are also noteworthy because they are taking place as the political far right is rising in popularity in France.

“Those parties, heading into France’s April 2027 election (not to mention Germany’s rolling election schedule), will seek to capitalize on the resentment that the violence of these protests has fostered and, if successful, to implement their anti-immigrant policy agenda,” he wrote.

An NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints is set to take place at the Stade de France just outside of the capital tomorrow, but the Ligue 1 top of the table clash between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon has been postponed.

The US Embassy in France issued a security alert on Thursday, warning American citizens in town for the game to “avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest.”

“Americans in Paris for the NFL game on Sunday, October 25 should also exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings,” the embassy said, warning that “recent demonstrations were violent and involved heavy property destruction, uncontrolled looting, and attacks on police.”

While the match is still scheduled to go ahead, a Steelers fan event in Paris was canceled by the NFL.

And PSG’s match against Lyon, originally scheduled for 8:45 p.m. local time on Sunday, has been postponed until Monday evening due to the expected protests in Paris. Several other soccer fixtures have been postponed too, including Toulouse FC’s match against ESTAC Troyes, and Montpellier Hérault SC’s Ligue 2 clash against Red Star FC.

Around 550,000 people attended the massive demonstrations across France that took place last Saturday, according to the country’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, marking one of the largest days of protest in France in recent years.

Hundreds were arrested, as violence broke out at several protests across the country. Catch up on what took place:

Before the demonstrations even began, fires were burning in the cities of Paris and Marseille. Police fired tear gas towards crowds in Paris and Lyon , charging into protest areas multiple times.

Though the protests were acknowledged by authorities as largely peaceful , in Lyon, a tourist office was set on fire , while demonstrators also broke into city halls in Marseille and Lille, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV.

As demonstrators in Paris reached the final destination of their march, large groups of young people were seen looting and starting fires where the protest began.

A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there, a police source told CNN affiliate BFMTV. There were no further details of how the incident occurred.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence , saying that those who attacked government buildings and businesses would be “prosecuted and punished.” There is “no room for violence in our Republic,” he said in a social media post .

CNN’s August Phillips, Joseph Ataman, Elina Baudier Kim and Charlotte Reck contributed to this reporting.

The kids are not alright. Across Europe, young people are protesting issues ranging from a lack of funding for education to the cost of housing, posing massive challenges to governments already under pressure and providing a visible sign of the intergenerational frustration felt by Gen Z.

The precise configuration of these grievances vary from country to country. Despite their different catalysts, however, all these movements have acted as a sort of black hole, drawing in any discontent before exploding in a catch-all outburst of frustration for a generation of young people who fear they won’t have the same opportunities as their parents.

They have, in part, inspired each other, too. Protesters in Italy and Greece have referenced their French counterparts in their slogans. Housing protests in Spain spilled over into Portugal. And student unions across Europe are sharing advice and their experiences with one another, Alice de Brito, vice president of France’s main student union, UNEF, told CNN.

For Julius Fintelmann, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of the European Correspondent daily newsletter, the protests “reflect a kind of frustration, the feeling that Europe’s politics is failing to deliver for the next generation.”

As well as education and housing, he points to an increasingly uncertain job market, where artificial intelligence disproportionately affects entry-level jobs, and the climate crisis as laying the groundwork for this explosion of Gen Z anger.

A few minutes past 2 p.m. local time and the main protest march has begun on the edge of Paris. The gathering here was marked by confusion and anger after the police banned the previously agreed protest route yesterday, booting the march to the city’s border, far away from its commercial and political centres.

The authorities were surely hoping to keep the protest out of sight and out of trouble today but the anger among people in France, especially young people, hasn’t been dimmed by the violence around last week’s protest.

There were no sign of tensions that marked the beginning of last week’s march, as students today called for the government to take seriously their demands for greater funding in education.

Peaceful protest marches are underway elsewhere in France, especially in the city of Orléans where the far right is holding a party congress this weekend.

Thousands of protesters have gathered in the French city of Orléans today to protest against the far-right National Rally party, which is holding its congress there this weekend.

About 11,000 people had joined the demonstration by midday, local authorities estimated, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV. Some marched holding cardboard signs, with slogans like “Racism is a crime” and “When protesting is no longer a right it is duty,” according to Reuters.

“We are here because for us the National Rally will never be a party like the others,” Sophie Binet, general secretary of France’s main union CGT, said at the protest. “It is a racist, antisemitic, and sexist party.”

Amid the scores of protesters expected to take to the streets across France today are the gilets jaunes , or Yellow Vests, part of a grassroots citizens’ movement that began almost a decade ago.

The movement dates back to 2018, when more than 250,000 people protested a rise in fuel tax announced by the government, which it said was to fight against climate change.

The protests – named after the yellow high-visibility jackets French motorists must carry in their vehicles – morphed into broader demonstrations against French President Emmanuel Macron and his government in the weeks following November 2018.

They often turned violent, with at least 10 people dying in connection with the protests in their first six weeks.

The French government made many concessions in the first weeks of the initial Yellow Vest protests, including scrapping the initial fuel tax, and implementing a 10 billion euro ($11.05 billion) package of wage rises and tax relief for the poorest.

The Yellow Vests have taken to the streets several times since those first protests died down. In 2020, police took more than 250 people in for questioning and fired tear gas during violent scenes involving the movement in Paris.

People from across the political spectrum have taken part in Yellow Vest protests, including anarchists, anti-immigration populists and hard-core fascists.

There are even groups on social media claiming to be environmental “yellow jackets,” a contradiction of the original protesters’ demands to scrap a new eco-tax.

Some have blamed a radical fringe of the Yellow Vest movement for a rise in anti-semitism in France.

A 2019 study conducted by the Fondation Jean Jaures showed that 50% of those who participated said they believed in a “global Zionist conspiracy.”

CNN’s Melissa Bell, Saskya Vandoorne and Gianluca Mezzofiore contributed to this reporting.

Like France, Italy is also braced for protests today with some shopkeepers in Milan, Rome and Florence boarding up their stores, and more police patrolling the streets than normal in the capital city.

Rome is decidedly on edge, with police in place ahead of an anti-war demonstration scheduled for 3 p.m. local time, which organizers expect 10,000 people to attend.

Two other demonstrations are still yet to be finalized, with organizers saying they will announce gathering points at the last minute.

Elsewhere in Milan, which witnessed two consecutive nights of unrest last weekend, people told CNN the mood didn’t feel especially tense as tourists and locals went about their daily routines.

In Naples, the US embassy has issued an alert, advising people to stay away from the Piazza Garibaldi, Piazza del Gesù, Palazzo San Giacomo and Castel Volturno in case of any protests.

CNN’s Barbie Latza Nadeau, Angelgabriel Pascuzzogonzalez, Stefano Pozzebon, Antonia Mortensen and Sharon Braithwaite contributed to this post.

articles.title: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father
articles.summary: The Met said it passed information to the duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
articles.body:
A letter making a "number of claims" relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, Scotland Yard has confirmed.

The Met said it passed the information relating to allegations outside the UK to the office of the Duke and Duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.

It was reported on Friday that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle, 82, had been found in his former home in the Philippines. Markle, who is based in the US, denies possessing any such images.

On Friday, Meghan said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. The Met said it was reviewing the matter and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog.

Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father

Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess said "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time".

The claims were first carried by the Sun newspaper, which later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against Markle.

In a statement, Scotland Yard said: "Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

"It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

"The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

"The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach."

Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.

In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.

The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.

The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.

They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

articles.title: France unrest: 70,000 police officers, weapons seized, hundreds of protesters arrested - top developments
articles.summary: France mobilised a massive security force on Saturday as protests over school funding, wages and soaring living costs spread across the country, a week
articles.body: France mobilised a massive security force on Saturday as protests over school funding, wages and soaring living costs spread across the country, a week after violent unrest left shops looted, cars burned and public buildings damaged.Authorities restricted a major march in Paris to the city’s southeastern edge, closed prominent museums and banned demonstrations in several cities to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence. Protesters carried banners with sayings like "We are fed up" and called for Macron's resignation.Police said that 110,000 people marched in the protestUp to 70,000 police officers deployedBefore the protests began, interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said that up to 70,000 officers would be deployed nationwide, supported by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. Security was tightened in Paris and other major cities after more than half a million people took to the streets the previous Saturday.These massive security arrangements came in the backdrop of last weekend when around 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted during last weekend’s unrest. Nuñez acknowledged on Monday that police had lost control in some cities during the violence. He offered to resign, but President Emmanuel Macron refused.Hundreds arrestedFrench police arrested 135 people in connection with protests and seized various weapons, French iterior minister Laurent Nuñez said, as authorities stepped up security amid fears of renewed violence.Police estimated that 110,000 people took part in the protest in Paris demanding increased school funding and opposing the rising cost of living. The march, seen as a show of strength against President Emmanuel Macron's government, leading to police firing tear gas and using water cannon. Despite rain and official restrictions confining the march to a route away from the city centre, large numbers turned out for the demonstration.Paris march restricted to city’s southeastern edgeParis police changed the route of a union-organised march on Friday, replacing the planned Bastille-to-Nation route with one between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes on the capital’s southeastern edge, reported AP.At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to instruct people to leave or face a 135-euro fine. The route restrictions were imposed to keep demonstrators away from central areas affected by last weekend’s violence.Paris police ordered a union-organised march to be moved at the last minute from central Bastille to Porte d’Italie on the capital’s southeastern outskirts. Unions reluctantly agreed to the change, while the Yellow Vests, the protest movement that staged disruptive demonstrations against Macron eight years ago, indicated they would defy the order.Major museums close as shopkeepers board up storesMajor Paris landmarks, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais, were closed on Saturday amid security concerns. The Grand Palais is hosting a major Cézanne exhibition.Art Basel, a prominent contemporary art fair, opened to the public on Friday but cancelled its weekend programme because of the threat of unrest.Shopkeepers across Paris also boarded up storefronts ahead of the demonstrations. Near Saint-Lazare train station, contractor Akram Ahmed, 34, was securing an optician’s shop on Saturday. “I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”Some demonstrations banned, teargas usedProtest marches were scheduled in Paris and Marseille, while local authorities banned some rallies in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier. French media reported that police used tear gas in Lyon on Saturday morning to disperse demonstrators. Later, it was reported that tear gas was used in several other cities as well.Police fired tear gas at protesters in Lyon, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes, hours after Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned, "We will not tolerate any violence or any disturbance of public order."Trade unions criticised the bans, describing them as violations of freedom of expression, a right protected by the French constitution.The restrictions came as authorities sought to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence, which saw masked groups target businesses and public buildings across the country.Thousands rally in OrléansThousands of people marched in Orléans, about 110 kilometres (70 miles) south of Paris to protest against the far right. The demonstration took place alongside a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party ahead of next spring’s presidential election.The rally added to a day of demonstrations across France, where public anger over living costs and public services has increasingly intersected with political tensions.Students and workers demand better schools, higher wagesThe protests began last month over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris but have since expanded into a broader movement over living standards.Student groups are demanding 250,000 additional higher-education places and an end to selection through Parcoursup, France’s national university admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.Students are seeking additional financial support, including an extra 200 euros a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing. Workers and unions are demanding higher wages and pensions to help households cope with rising costs.“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”Protesters were also seen holding a sign reading "We are fed up" during one of the many demonstrations.Macron faces pressure as protests widenThe demonstrations have added to pressure on Macron during the final stretch of his current presidency, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017.Macron met high school representatives on Friday, who said he had promised to overhaul the university admissions system. However, they called for protests to continue until concrete measures were formally announced.The government has defended restrictions on demonstrations as necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, as France faces mounting anger over living costs and public services.Protesters have also called for Macron's resignation. Far-left French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined demonstrators at the front of an authorised protest in Paris, praised the turnout and urged President Emmanuel Macron to heed the protesters' demands. "There is a magnificent mass response, showing collective discipline and self-control. I think he [Emmanuel Macron] will realise that this is going to happen every week - it's time for him to give in," he said, warning that demonstrations would continue every week unless Macron backed down. "Don’t add fuel to the fire, stop trying to pit people against each other," he added.Europe on the boil: Protests in Italy, Spain & moreItaly deployed an additional 500 soldiers to Milan ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, a week after looting and clashes with police. The deployment, announced by Premier Giorgia Meloni, came alongside tighter security measures, including drone surveillance, railway station checks and rapid-response units. Around 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel were expected to support security operations in the city.In Rome, authorities tightened security around luxury shopping streets and major public spaces ahead of planned demonstrations, including an anti-war march and a rally by right-wing students. Protests were also scheduled in several other Italian cities amid concerns over possible violence.In Albania, student-led protesters planned a fresh anti-government rally in the capital, Tirana, on Saturday after days of violent unrest. Demonstrators have demanded better education facilities, lower tuition fees and action against corruption, while also calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. More than 300 people, including police officers, have been injured since the protests began, according to AFP. Although tensions had eased in recent days, organisers urged students and other groups to join the latest rally.Meanwhile, thousands of retirees and supporters marched in Spain capital to demand protection for public pensions ahead of next month’s snap election. In Lisbon, protesters prepared to march for affordable housing, opposing government measures they say could leave tenants more vulnerable to rent increases and eviction.Protests also erupted in Belgium, where police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed with anti-government demonstrators in Brussels on Saturday. Hundreds of mainly young protesters gathered to demand increased education funding and accuse police of excessive violence. Clashes broke out as officers pursued demonstrators, with Reuters witnesses reporting that police hit and kicked one protester. articles.title: Ukraine reports Starlink operating again after slowdown
articles.summary: Ukraine’s Starlink satellite links have been restored after the country experienced limitations with accessing this critical technology, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced Saturday. SpaceX’s military-grade version of Starlink, called Starshield, supports Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. Zelensky confirmed the restoration in a statement shared on social media Saturday afternoon local time. “The speeds are now…
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Starlink satellite links have been restored after the country experienced limitations with accessing this critical technology, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced Saturday.

SpaceX’s military-grade version of Starlink, called Starshield, supports Ukraine’s drone operations and communication.

Zelensky confirmed the restoration in a statement shared on social media Saturday afternoon local time.

“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said in the statement. “The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered ‘shaheds.'”

The Ukrainian leader thanked “all Americans” and partners who assisted in this effort, including U.S. lawmakers, the State Department, the media and Trump.

Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters on a call that the ministry’s monitoring systems now reported stable connections for objects traveling faster than around 250 miles per hour.

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield,” Khmara told reporters, according to Reuters. “We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable.”

Khmara attributed the change to “ direct dialogue ” between Zelensky and the Trump administration. He added that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

This announcement follows tensions between Kyiv and the U.S. over President Trump’s Russian diesel deal and decision to postpone sanctions on Moscow — two decisions Zelensky warned endangered Ukrainians in their ongoing war against Russia.

Zelensky said in Friday remarks that Ukraine’s military was still struggling with Starlink satellite speeds limited at around 100 mph.

“The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there, and the speed has not been restored,” the Ukrainian president said.

Earlier that day, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had not spoken with SpaceX leader Elon Musk about the restricted Starlink speeds in Ukraine but said he “might have to” if the issue was not fixed.

This week, Russia accepted an invitation to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart talks after Nov. 10, according to his foreign affairs adviser.

Additionally, the White House said Friday that first lady Melania Trump helped secure a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that will begin Thursday in the front-line city of Oleshky.

This action will “allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” according to the White House.

articles.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale
articles.summary: The Geordie singer says on Instagram he is "not happy" with the reported ticket prices.
articles.body:
Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.

"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."

He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.

Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.

The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

articles.title: 'Kaam kar diya hai': Haryana student beaten with iron rod, sticks; CCTV captures nearly 50 blows in a minute
articles.summary: BHIWANI: A BBA student was allegedly subjected to a brutal, life-threatening assault in Haryana’s Bhiwani district, after being knocked off his motorcycle
articles.body: BHIWANI: A BBA student was allegedly subjected to a brutal, life-threatening assault in Haryana’s Bhiwani district, after being knocked off his motorcycle by a car and attacked with sticks and an iron rod in the middle of the road.CCTV footage of the incident has surfaced, purportedly showing three assailants involved in the attack. According to the victim’s family, nearly 50 blows were inflicted on him within a minute, leaving him with serious injuries and six fractures.The victim, identified as Rudra, is a resident of Paluwas village in Bhiwani district.According to his father, Vinod, the incident took place around 7 pm near Hudda Park, close to Paluwas turn. Rudra was riding his motorcycle when a blue car allegedly struck him from behind, knocking him onto the road.Vinod alleged that three men stepped out of the car after Rudra fell and attempted to forcibly take him away. When the student resisted, the assailants allegedly pulled out sticks and an iron rod and launched a vicious assault on him.The CCTV footage shows two men repeatedly striking Rudra while a third appears to be holding him.Rudra allegedly managed to break free and tried to flee, but the attackers chased him and caught him again.His father further alleged that the assailants pointed a pistol at the student. After the attack, the accused allegedly made a video call to someone and declared, “Rudra ka kaam kar diya hai” (Rudra has been finished). They then fled the scene in their car.The family also alleged that Rudra repeatedly cried out for help, but passers-by did not intervene. Motorcyclists, motorists and pedestrians reportedly continued to pass the spot while the student was being assaulted.Vinod suspects that the attack was triggered by an earlier dispute involving his elder son, Dhruv. According to him, an altercation had taken place around one-and-a-half months ago between Dhruv and some associates of the accused. The family believes that the old dispute may have led the attackers to target Rudra.Vinod alleged that the assailants attacked his son with the intention of inflicting severe injuries. articles.title: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.summary: US intelligence memo warns that Iranian plots against US citizens in the Middle East ‘have reached advanced stages’.
articles.body:
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).

The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.

The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.

Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:

What has the US said about Iran’s alleged plans to attack Americans?

A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.

In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.

The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.

The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.

What evidence has Washington presented, and what remains unverified?

Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.

Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.

Why have US officials raised the alarm now?

According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.

This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.

In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month . On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.

Which countries has the US withdrawn diplomats from?

On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.

Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.

A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.

Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.

However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.

On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.

That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.

Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.

Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.

Has Iran previously been accused of plotting attacks against Americans?

Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.

In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.

An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.

Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani .

This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.
